name: Glass skin routine

card.summary: A K-beauty goal of poreless, translucent, glowing skin pursued through a multi-step routine; online it is as much an aesthetic ideal as a defined protocol, with no dedicated clinical studies.
card.note: A look and a routine style, not a clinical protocol; individual steps such as sunscreen and acne care are studied separately.

quick.overview:
Glass skin refers to a look of smooth, even, luminous skin that appears almost translucent, popularised through Korean skincare and social media. The associated routine layers many products such as oil and water cleansers, exfoliation, essences, ampoules, moisturiser and sunscreen.

On looksmax.org, users discuss it as both a goal and a routine, with posters debating how much depends on genetics versus diet and skincare. No published study evaluates the glass skin routine itself.
quick.mechanism: Posters describe a layered routine: double cleansing, gentle chemical exfoliation (BHA/AHA) about once a week, hydrating essences or ampoules, moisturiser and daily sunscreen, plus diet and hydration. The visual effect is attributed to hydration, even texture and reduced inflammation.
quick.risks: Overuse of exfoliating acids is a commonly discussed irritation risk, which some posters themselves caution against. Forum posts mix routine advice with dietary claims and talk of prescription acne drugs, which are outside the routine itself.

lead: Glass skin is a skincare goal from Korean beauty culture: skin that looks smooth, even, minimal in visible pores and faintly translucent, with a dewy sheen. People pursue it with a layered routine of cleansing, gentle exfoliation, hydrating essences or ampoules, moisturiser and daily sunscreen, aiming for a clearer, more luminous complexion that reads as healthy and youthful in person and in photos.[1]

Wikipedia describes the look as favoured in South Korea and achieved less through foundation than through a long skincare regimen focused on toning and clarifying, averaging around ten steps that start with a double cleanse and move through sheet masks, essences, serums and moisturiser to SPF sunscreen by day.[1] The term spread through K-beauty retailers, YouTube tutorials and social media, and on looksmax.org it appears both as a trend and as a routine people try to follow for acne and texture.[3][4][6]

No clinical study has tested a glass skin routine as a whole. Its individual parts are described in general skin care references: moisturisers raise skin water content, sunscreen protects against UV damage, and over-exfoliation can cause irritation and barrier damage.[5][10][12] Dermatological consensus summarised in those references favours a basic routine of gentle cleansing, moisturising and sun protection, with other products reserved for specific concerns.[5]

chain: Layered cleansing, hydration and sun protection
Even texture, less irritation and visible hydration
A smoother, glossier, more luminous complexion
angle.text: The routine aims at hydrated, calm, evenly textured skin that reflects light, which people describe as the glass look. Followers attribute the result to consistency with cleansing, hydration, gentle exfoliation and sunscreen.

paras: Wikipedia's K-beauty article describes a routine that begins with a double cleanse, continues through sheet masks, essences, lotions, serums and rich moisturisers, and ends with SPF sunscreen in the daytime or a thicker sleep cream at night.[1] A representative looksmax.org guide lists an oil-based cleanser, then a water-based cleanser, a BHA or AHA exfoliant about once a week, a moisturising essence, an ampoule, moisturiser and sunscreen, with a food list and advice to drink plenty of water.[3] Another poster describes a simpler acne-focused version: a foaming cleanser, a chemical exfoliant, avoiding physical scrubs while acne is active, plus diet and water changes.[4]

The look itself is defined by appearance rather than by ingredient: smooth surface texture, even tone, hydration that makes skin reflect light, and little visible redness or inflammation. Followers attribute the effect to hydration, evenness of texture and calm skin, rather than to makeup coverage.[1][3]

Korean beauty traces its roots to the Three Kingdoms period, with the Goryeo era regarded as a peak, and under the Joseon dynasty Confucian values favoured fair skin and cherry-red lips as marks of status.[1] Korean cosmetics historically drew on oils, plants and powders.[1]

The BB cream, a tinted skin-care base, was created in Germany in the 1960s by dermatologist Christine Schrammek to protect patients' skin after peels and surgery. Korean companies refined it in the 1980s, and by 2011 it accounted for 13 percent of South Korea's cosmetics market. Major Western brands launched their own versions from 2012, and some critics argued these were little more than tinted moisturiser.[8] The K-beauty article dates its arrival in Western markets to 2011, a claim flagged on that page as needing further sourcing.[1]

The Korean Wave, or Hallyu, the global spread of Korean dramas and music that began in the late 1990s and accelerated through the 2000s and 2010s, carried Korean beauty with it.[11] The 2014 drama My Love from the Star, sponsored by Amorepacific, was reported to lift skincare sales by up to 75 percent and lipstick by 400 percent.[1] In the United States, Korean American esthetician Charlotte Cho and her husband David co-founded the retailer Soko Glam in 2012, and her 2015 book The Little Book of Skin Care introduced routines to a Western audience; her Wikipedia biography credits her as a major contributor to K-beauty's rise in the US.[15]

Glass skin spread globally through social media as visual shorthand for the whole routine. Wikipedia notes rising UK demand for the glass skin look and cites Mintel data that about 68 percent of global skincare launches came from South Korea; Asia-Pacific held the largest K-beauty market share as of 2020.[1] Seoul's Gangnam district, a hub for dermatology and cosmetic procedures, and growing medical tourism are described alongside the home-care routine.[1]

General skin care references describe cleansers as removing oil, dirt and makeup with surfactants, with synthetic detergent cleansers milder than traditional alkaline soap.[5] Double cleansing pairs an oil-based cleanser, which followers say lifts sunscreen and sebum, with a water-based one.[3] The skin care article does not itself discuss double cleansing.[5]

Moisturisers work by humectants drawing water in, occlusives such as petrolatum slowing water loss, and emollients softening the surface; petrolatum is described as cutting transepidermal water loss by 50 to 75 percent for several hours.[12] Humectants work best when combined with occlusives, and no moisturiser format has been shown clearly more effective than others.[12] Hyaluronic acid is a common humectant ingredient that binds water because of its negative charge, though the encyclopedia article cites little direct trial evidence for topical hyaluronic acid moisturising.[14]

Sunscreen is the step with the most research behind appearance outcomes. Broad-spectrum products absorb or scatter UVA and UVB. A 2013 trial of about 900 Australians reported smoother, more resilient skin after 4.5 years of daily broad-spectrum sunscreen compared with controls, and a 32-person study reported reversal of photoaging within 12 weeks of daily SPF 30, according to the sunscreen article.[10] Health bodies commonly advise SPF 30 or higher and reapplication about every two hours.[10]

Chemical exfoliants (AHAs such as glycolic and lactic acid, BHAs such as salicylic acid) loosen bonds between dead skin cells; they are described as gentler than mechanical scrubs and are recommended for acne-prone skin, though dermatologists say exfoliation is not medically necessary because dead cells shed naturally, and over-exfoliation can weaken the barrier and cause tightness, redness and infection risk.[5][16] Niacinamide, a frequent serum ingredient, has tentative evidence for acne, hyperpigmentation and redness, with a 2 percent topical reducing sebum excretion over two to four weeks in one study the encyclopedia cites.[9]

Centella asiatica, often shortened to centella or cica in marketing, appears in looksmax.org replies as a source of the glassy finish.[6] A review summarised on Wikipedia describes traditional use for skin conditions and minor wounds, contact dermatitis as a possible effect of topical use, and states that clinical efficacy and safety have not been proven in clinical research.[13]

K-beauty staples named in reference works include sheet masks, essences, serums, cushion compacts, fermented products and night creams, with ingredients such as green tea, soybean, snail secretion, bee venom and pig collagen appearing in marketing.[1] Looksmax.org guides name an oil cleanser, a water-based cleanser, a weekly BHA or AHA exfoliant, an essence and an ampoule as the Korean-origin steps, with centella mentioned in one reply for a glassy finish.[3][6] A poster describing a six-month acne routine chose a foaming ceramide cleanser and a chemical exfoliant, and stressed avoiding physical scrubs while acne is active.[4] Further guides on the forum offer simplified glass-skin and anti-aging routines.[17][18]

Wikipedia's K-beauty article notes that appearance pressure around the industry can affect young people's self-esteem and that conformity pressure has been strong; it also describes the Korean 'Escape the Corset' movement, profiled by The New York Times in 2018, which challenges rigid beauty standards.[1] The article describes many Korean products as thoroughly regulated, and the US 2022 Modernization of Cosmetics Regulation Act as adding product listing and adverse-event reporting; the EU applies harmonised criteria to cosmetic claims.[1] 'Clean beauty' has no single legal definition.[1]

The skin care article notes that anti-aging and routine products are often marketed with unproven claims, that vague labels such as 'gentle' have no fixed meaning, and that social media routines have led some children and teens to use harsh or unnecessary products.[5] Men participate increasingly in K-beauty, though the market still centres on women.[1]

Forum threads on glass skin range from routine guides to before-and-after acne accounts.[3][4] One poster asked whether anyone had reached the look through lifestyle and skincare alone, suggesting people who have it often already had a good genetic base; a reply credited the product centella for the glassy finish.[6] A Lemmy skincare thread shows the same interest outside looksmaxxing, from a woman in her forties asking how to get the glassy look.[7]

Guides on looksmax.org typically blend topical steps with diet and water advice, and at least one before-and-after thread mentions prescription acne medication in passing; those drugs sit outside the routine itself.[3][4]
No studies found. The routine's individual components, such as sunscreen, retinoids or acne treatment, are studied separately in the dermatology literature but not as a glass skin protocol.

lore.intro: Glass skin is discussed on looksmax.org as both a K-beauty trend and a skincare goal, with threads giving routines and personal before-and-after accounts.[3][4][6]

claims.claim: Glass skin is achievable through a layered K-beauty routine.
claims.believers: Posters publish step lists of oil and water cleansing, weekly exfoliation, essence, ampoule and sunscreen, and one reports going from severe oily acne to clear skin over about six months with a cleanser, chemical exfoliant and diet changes.[3][4]
claims.experts: No published study has tested the glass skin routine as a whole; individual steps are evaluated separately in dermatology.[5]

claims.claim: Specific foods and heavy water intake produce clearer, glassy skin.
claims.believers: A forum guide lists foods such as walnuts, avocado and tomatoes as helpful, and advises avoiding fried food, sugar, cheese and coffee, while another thread recommends several litres of water daily.[3][4]
claims.experts: No published studies were found linking the foods or water volumes in these posts to a glass skin look.

claims.claim: The glass look depends largely on genetics, with routine changing one or two things
claims.believers: One poster argues people with the look usually had a strong genetic base and only needed to stop habits such as sugar binging.[6]
claims.experts: No published study has examined how much of the glass skin appearance is attributable to genetics versus routine.

claims.claim: Centella gives skin the glassy look
claims.believers: A looksmax.org reply states 'the glass look is from a product called centella', which the poster uses for moisturisation and as an anti-inflammatory.[6]
claims.experts: Wikipedia's summary of the research says clinical efficacy and safety of Centella asiatica for skin have not been proven in clinical research, and notes contact dermatitis from topical use.[13]

claims.claim: Daily sunscreen is a core part of getting and keeping glass skin
claims.believers: Guides list sunscreen as the final daytime step of the routine and K-beauty descriptions end the day routine with SPF.[1][3]
claims.experts: A 2013 trial of about 900 Australians reported smoother, more resilient skin after 4.5 years of daily broad-spectrum sunscreen, according to Wikipedia's sunscreen article.[10]

claims.claim: Exfoliating with BHA/AHA, but not scrubs, clears texture without damage
claims.believers: Forum guides advise chemical exfoliation about once a week and warn against physical scrubs for acne-prone skin, saying scrubs intensify inflammation.[3][4]
claims.experts: Wikipedia's exfoliation article says chemical exfoliants are recommended for acne but that dermatologists regard exfoliation as not medically necessary, and that excessive exfoliation can weaken the barrier.[16]

claims.claim: A long multi-step routine is needed for the look
claims.believers: K-beauty descriptions and forum guides present steps such as double cleansing, essence, ampoule and moisturiser as the route to the look.[1][3]
claims.experts: Skin care references summarise dermatological consensus as favouring a basic routine of gentle cleansing, moisturising and sun protection.[5]
